## Reviewer #2
## (Remarks to the Author)

This manuscript aims to generate a spatial map of gene expression (using tomo-seq) and epigenetic features such as chromosome accessibility (ATAC-seq) and bioinformatically predicted TF binding sites in chick embryos at primitive streak and early neurulation stages, to try to uncover spatial patterns of gene regulation in the embryo. The paper then explores some effects of exposing cells to activation of Wnt, as a putative posteriorizing factor. The data are important and interesting and should be a very useful resource for the community and to prompt further studies, coupled to embryological knowledge and future cell biology studies.

The title promised a very interesting and provocative story and given the lab's long track record of beautiful papers, I expected that it would contain a major discovery about gene regulatory patterns in space and time that would presage the acquisition of cell positional identity at a later moment in developmental time. Unfortunately, the paper does not deliver this. The main problem is some misinterpretation of the topology of the embryo at these stages in relation to time (ie. the spacetime relationships of cells), which seriously affects the interpretation of the key findings and generating incorrect conclusions.

Most of the studies have been done at HH stage 5, when the primitive streak has reached its full length and the head process (cranial part of the notochord) has emerged, with the prechordal mesendoderm at its tip (by the way this is not the "gastrula" stage but early neurula, because the future neural plate is already thickening at this stage and will start to elevate soon afterwards - but this is not so important). What is more important is that if an embryo at this stage is sectioned transversely (at right angles to the primitive streak and head process), these coordinates do not entirely correspond to the "anterior-posterior" axis in terms of cell identities or fates. From the tip of the primitive streak forwards, where the neural plate starts to form, yes indeed, this is the future head neuroectoderm and there the positions of cells do roughly correspond to their future rostrocaudal identities (forebrain to mid-hindbrain). But from the node down, the positions of cells at this stage do not correspond to the future "anterior-posterior" axis but much more closely to a temporal axis. It is true that the future tail will form at the most extreme posterior level of this, but the cells occupying this position in the epiblast as well as mesoderm at this stage are mainly lateral (mesoderm) and extraembryonic rather than posterior. Gradually as the streak shortens, the a/p axis of both the epiblast and the underlying mesoderm become more coincident, again the region in front of the node. In fact, some cells just emerging from the middle of the primitive streak at HH5 will end up in quite anterior positions in the mesoderm, as this tissue moves both away from the midline and anteriorly concomitantly to the narrowing and extension of the whole embryo. For these reasons, the sequential set of sections analyzed only correspond to the future a-p/cranialcaudal axis (in terms of cell identity) in the most anterior parts. Thus, the finding that in the most anterior sections there are many genes with differential expression corresponding to their final positions, whereas in the posterior sections there are very few, is not surprising - it is exactly what would be expected. It does not, as the text states, reveal an "unexpected regulatory complexity in the anterior gastrula". Genes like Cdx4 and Wnt5A "move" back with the elongating axis, marking a moving state rather than a cell identity - as cells move out of this domain they switch off these markers and acquire their positional characteristics. In other words, the a-p axis of the embryo at this stage, at least from the node downwards, is more like a temporal axis than a spatial one. So a series of cartesian coordinates does not accurately represent the embryonic organization or the future identity of the cells located in different positions, and different sections are not equivalent to each other.

Similar problems apply to the earlier embryos studied. At what the authors call "HH stage 1" [which actually no longer exists - this stage has been replaced by a series of 14 stages described by Eyal-Giladi and Kochav in 1976 so HH1 is no longer used/useful], cells are undergoing major reorganization within the epiblast and the most lateral cells in the disc will come to occupy the most "posterior" positions at the time of primitive streak formation. These are the well described "polonaise" movements. So again, a series of cartesian coordinates of embryos at these stages does not reflect future positional identities.

The "a-p patterning" literature, mainly in amphibians, contains evidence for at least 3 separate signals involved in "posteriorization": Wnt, FGF and retinoic acid. They probably are all involved in this, but in different regions of the axis and possibly in different germ layers. (in fact, such "posteriorization" is in principle incompatible with the authors' chosen alternative model, Mangold's idea of separate organizers for different parts of the axis). The paper looks at aspects of Wnt and its relation to their proposed pCREs (positional regulatory elements). Interesting and useful data using CUT&RUN with the Wnt target LEF/CTNNB1 are provided, in 3 regions of the embryo. Wnt signals are enriched in the most posterior but again this is likely to be related to the comparatively younger state of the epiblast and mesoderm in these regions relative to the maturing early neural plate at the other end and the authors' experiments do not allow these to be disentangled. The remaining experiments are done on dissociated cells in vitro (from the anterior part of the embryo at HH2, corresponding to the early gastrulation stage when the primitive streak starts to form), treated with Wnt modulators. There are differences between gain and loss of function, not surprisingly, but again the biological meaning of these changes cannot be resolved in terms of temporal/maturation versus axial identity. Moreover the cells appear to include all germ layers which complicates things further. The choice of tissue as the source of these cells is rather odd - this is not the region of the embryo that is likely to be patterned (posteriorized) by Wnt, certainly not the mesoderm, since at HH2 the anterior half of the embryo has very few if any mesoderm cells. One possibility is that the treatments can generate some mesoderm from epiblast. The hypoblast is also likely to be present in these dissociated samples. So very difficult to interpret unambiguously.

Finally, the authors use single cell multi-omics using 10X genomics for RNAseq and ATAC. Another useful dataset, but also again a problem with interpretation. It is not surprising that there are clusters of like-cells, some of them probably identifiable from their signatures, but these results fit with many different interpretations. The authors claim that they support the proposal in the title.

I think the authors have been led astray by these results. Interestingly, a similar problem affects another relatively recent paper (Metzis et al., cited in this paper) partly for the same reasons ("anterior" in the paper is mainly neural plate, "posterior" is mainly a mixture of things, and what the paper calls "neural induction" is in fact the start of the later events of neuronal differentiation, characterized by the expression of neuronal, rather than neural plate, markers). I bring this up in this review because it is a good example of how the title of a paper can be taken for granted and propagate through the literature.

I do feel that this study does contain some very interesting data, and that the authors have indeed opened up an interesting question that is certainly worth pursuing. But I think that in order to do this appropriately, experiments need to be designed that take into account the temporal and spatial organization of the embryo itself as a guide, rather than imprint upon it human-generated systems of orthogonal coordinates that do not correspond to the underlying biological organization. I encourage the authors to re-think this story. The results are worth publishing in some form, but the interpretation needs to be seriously revised. The question of whether there is a general pre-pattern of chromatin organization that prefigures axial patterning, as already demonstrated 40 years ago for the Hox clusters, is indeed a good one and the authors are encouraged to explore this further in future studies.
## Reviewer #3
## (Remarks to the Author)

To discover whether and how positional information is recorded in the epigenome during embryo pattern formation, the authors took advantage of the large size of avian embryos, generated abundant data from spatial transcriptomic and epigenomic techniques, and performed comprehensive analyses. In the avian gastrula, the authors observed that some positional CREs (pCREs) formed gradients of chromatin accessibility (assessed by ATAC-seq) along the anterior-posterior axis. By unbiased clustering, they identified two sets of pCREs: anterior and posterior pCREs, on which the chromatin accessibility and the chromatin activity (assessed by H3K27ac CUT&RUN) are significantly higher at the anterior and posterior poles of the gastrula, respectively. They claimed that polarization of chromatin activity on these two pCRE sets precedes the spatial patterning of gene expression, and the pCRE gradients are shaped by signaling pathways, such as the WNT pathway, at the onset of gastrulation. Interestingly, the authors found that anterior and posterior pCREs can be used to predict the location of cells following the anterior-posterior axis not only in the entire embryo but also within individual germ layers. Overall, this manuscript is well prepared and nicely illustrated. However, there are several points the authors need to address to enhance the organization of the manuscript and better substantiate their conclusions.

1. line 143-148: Data indicated here (Fig. S4, Fig. S5, Fig. 2G) are merely generated from eight peaks in the OTX2 locus and eight peaks in the WNT5A locus. The authors need to include data from all anterior and posterior pCREs, such as Fig. S6. Moreover, can the authors explain what the criteria were for selecting these 16 peaks?
2. line 148-150: Can the authors show evidence of this restriction? If not, this conclusion should be removed.
3. line 160-162: Without more data or statistical analyses, it’s difficult to tell if AP gene sets get regionalized following/after the establishment of pCRE gradients in Fig. S6. Please elaborate.
4. line 165-166: This conclusion is overstated if only data on individual gene loci are shown.

5. line 177: Why were HH5 embryos used for LEF1/CTNNB1 CUT&RUN? To test whether WNT signaling factors regulate pCRE gradients, CUT&RUN needs to be performed no later than when pCRE is spatially activated, which is the HH3 stage according to line 158. Otherwise, it’s difficult to distinguish between direct effects and indirect effects.
6. line 183-184: This conclusion is overstated considering my previous comment.
7. line 199-200: Statistical analysis is needed to support this claim.

8. Fig. 2E: Please highlight anterior and posterior pCRE clusters and move other clusters to supplemental figures. Moreover, the authors are encouraged to include additional analyses to strengthen the biological significance of anterior and posterior pCRE clusters, such as the expression positioning of pCRE-associated genes (current Fig. 4C-D), the relationship between pCRE-associated genes and the 706/294 anteriorly/posteriorly enriched genes, as well as GREAT GO analysis of pCREs.
9. Fig. 3J,K: Please separately indicate WNT-responsive and -inhibitory peaks/profiles.
10. Fig. 4C,D: These two panels are suggested to move to Fig. 2 or Fig. 2 related supplemental figures.
11. Fig. 5D: Mislabeled markers.
12. Fig. 5F,G: These two panels do not belong to this figure.
13. Fig. S6: Mislabeled y-axis in the right part.

(Remarks to the Author) The authors have addressed most of the concerns/issues raised by Reviewer 2 in the rebuttal and with the revision of the manuscript.
There are issues on “the significance of these putative coordinates” and “toned down interpretation” that may need further clarification.
Significance of the putative coordinates (or “positional information is encoded within the chromatin landscape” – Abstract).

As previously pointed out by Reviewer 1, the information (regionalised gene expression pattern and active CREs in the accessible chromatin region) collated from the TomoRNA-seq and TomoATAC-Seq datasets reflects the composition of cell types of a multitude of cell populations localized in different regions of the HH5 avian embryo. The CRE profile does not by default carry any positional information of the descendants of the cell population along the A-P axis in the final body plan. The spatial pattern of the expression of the TomoRNA-seq gene set that is characteristic of the cell types in the regionalized cell populations of interest and together with the sets of CREs that display peak-gene co-accessibility (e.g. Fig 4C, D) provided the spatial register (positional address) of the different cell types in the whole embryo or the germ layer (e.g., Fig. 5). Based on this register, single cells from the embryos at the same developmental stage can be mapped to the inferred positions in the embryo (re Fig. 4- the legend may be revised as “region-related CREs enable inferring the position of cells in the embryo”). The primary attribute (“significance”) of the spatial register, or measurable positional values information (line 67) is for inferring (not “can predict” – Line 67) where in the germ layers individual cells reside within the embryo (e.g., Fig 4B, 5C). This approach meets the requirement of identifying the spatial position of cell clusters in the embryo, without resorting to high-resolution spatial multi-omics analysis. Mapping of single cells to the specific germ layer population in the embryo facilitates the clustering of the single cells by markers genes (e.g. Fig S10), and the follow-on elucidation of the enrichment of CREs in these populations (e.g. Fig. S11).

The terminology anterior pCREs and posterior pCREs potentially lead to misconstruing the measurable positional values reflects the final positional address of the specific cell population in the body axes (as articulated in the first two paragraphs of Introduction). To avoid such misconstruing, it may be appropriate to revise the Introduction by removing the first two paragraphs and go straightly with the third paragraph. Since the “anterior: a” and “posterior: p” descriptors are based on the anatomical/topographical position of the cell population with refence to a morphological landmark (Hensen’s Node of HH5 embryo), it may be appropriate to name these CREs as regional CRE (rCRE) with designation of aN-rCREs and pN-rCREs (aN and pN stand for anterior to node: AP1, AP2, and posterior to node: AP3-7 Fig 2A). This would help distinguishing these regional CREs from those that are truly positional CREs (pCRE) of axial identity genes (e.g., pCREs of members of HOX gene clusters displaying different expression domain in the A-P axis, Fig. 1F, 2G, 3E), in the discussion about the axial information recorded in the chromatin landscape / epigenome (line 176-180, line 269-274, Fig 4F, G - HH10 embryo)
Toned down the interpretation of the CRE functionality.

The most impactful findings of this study are the characterization of the epigenome landscape/architecture of the germ layers of HH5 embryo at spatial resolution, and the identification of the CREs of different functionality (e.g., Supp Fig S3). In this context, while arguably that functional analysis of HH5 CREs is outside the scope of this study (apart from the demonstration of changes in CRE activity of HH2 epiblast cells in response to modulated WNT signalling activity), further functional annotation of the CRE sets would enhance the merit of this study on CRE functions. In a similar study of mouse gastrula embryo, a range of CRE functionality has been identified, including driving cell lineage development, anterior-posterior patterning, response to long-range signalling activity and short-range signalling activity and cell-cell interaction, midline mesendoderm formation, mesoderm patterning, cell cycle control and others. Of interest is the scope of functionality of the germ layer-specific CREs, as well as specifically those enriched CRs that are related to genes that display overlapping spatially-restricted expression across different germ layers (e.g., Fig S11D for ectoderm-mesoderm, yet missing the data for ectoderm-endoderm and endoderm-mesoderm). Together, knowledge gleaned from this study would deeper insights into the molecular architecture and functional attributes of the gene regulatory networks of lineage specification and differentiation and tissue patterning in the developing embryo.

This additional information may help to justify the interpretation of CREs of developmental genes that displayed spatially restricted expression domain actively record the positional information shared by distinct cell types and across populations in different germ layers (line 345-354) and that CREs regulated by nuclear effectors of signalling pathways provide the readout of the mechanistic guidance for tissue patterning in the A-P axis (line 359-374).

Regarding the assertion that results of this study inform how cells are allocated to positional (anterior or posterior) fate during development, further clarification may be required to identify which results are showing the spatiotemporal changes in epigenomic states for both anterior and posterior axis identity (or cell fates) are established early in development (line 375382, line 390-392), and that the epigenome stores the positional information, as records of morphogen-derived signals into chromatin accessibility landscape or positional references for downstream GRN activity (for early specification of correct axial cell types, line 396-399), during early development. Of note: the developmental series of embryos analysed for this study was incomplete (Fig. S6), which was missing HH4 when further activation of CREs (both those that are concomitant with expression of target genes and preceding gene expression, e.g. Fig. S7) may happen.

It is of interest to demonstrate conservation of CRE signatures, but the study may go further to demonstrate conservation of functionality to account for species-specific difference in functionality of certain conserved CREs. As the comparative study covered only two species (both are amniote), it would not be appropriate to extend the findings to conservation across all vertebrates. Reviewer 3 previously queried the merit/relevance of the conservation study. Given that the study was limited to two species and it is unclear if the tissue constitution of the germ layers and the spatial pattern of gene expression are comparable/conserved between HH5 avian embryo and E7.5 mouse embryo, it may be appropriate to remove these results (and discussion, line339-403) and include them for a more in-depth study across a range of developmental stages of these two species as well as including other vertebrate model organisms.

It is more likely that the definitive endoderm has yet to be specified and the “endoderm” in the posterior region is the descendant of the hypoblast.
